Shot at real DFW events

What the cloud actually looks like on a dance floor

Every clip below is from a booking we ran. No stock footage, no renders, nothing bought from a library. Six rooms, and no room twice: a daylight greenhouse, a grand ballroom, a stone hall, an uplit chapel, a live band on a stage and a rustic barn. Watch what the fog does at floor level, how flat it stays while people move through it, and how the colour in the room reads back out of the cloud.

The effect, by the name most people use

Dancing on the clouds

Dancing on the clouds is a knee-deep layer of white fog laid flat across the dance floor. It does not rise, it does not haze the room, and it does not drift into the tables. The couple stands above it rather than inside it, which is the whole point, from the front row and from the photographer’s position, the floor disappears and the two of you appear to be standing on a cloud.

It works because the fog is chilled. Warm fog rises and fills a room; cold fog sinks and stays. All four of our sizes do that same job by a slightly different route, three chill the fog by passing it through a basket of dry ice, and the fourth chills it with an onboard ultrasonic water system and no dry ice at all.

People search for this effect under half a dozen names, dancing on the clouds, a cloud machine, low lying fog, ground fog, dry ice fog, a low fog machine for a first dance. They are all the same look. What differs is which machine gets used, how long the cloud holds, and whether anyone is standing there running it.

A dry ice cloud lasts exactly as long as the dry ice load lasts. Nothing else about the machine changes that.

The one thing nobody tells you before you book
The part that decides everything

How long the cloud actually lasts

This is the question that matters and it is the one almost no rental listing answers. A dry ice cloud machine works by dropping a basket of dry ice into heated water. Fog is produced for as long as there is ice in the basket. When the ice is gone, the cloud stops, not gradually, not with a warning, just stops. So the honest answer to “how long does it last” is not a number printed on a machine. It is however long the ice load in that particular machine lasts, at the output level it is being run at.

Which means the size of the ice basket is the specification that actually governs your event. A machine with a small basket can carry one song beautifully. A machine with a large basket can carry a grand entrance walk, hold through the introductions, and still have ice left for the first dance. Running a small machine hard to cover a long moment is exactly how people end up with a cloud that dies halfway through the chorus.

So it is easier to think of what we own as four sizes of the same effect rather than four machines, a ladder from one defining moment up to all night long. One of them comes to your event. These are the four rungs, smallest load to largest.

Nimbus JuniorSize 01 · 8 lb dry ice

One defining moment. Intimate floors, small chapels, tight reception rooms where a large machine has nowhere to sit.

NimbusSize 02 · 12 lb dry ice

The workhorse, and what most weddings book. Longer hold, and enough in the basket to cover back-to-back dances rather than one.

ADJ Entour IceSize 03 · 30 lb dry ice · DMX

The largest load we carry, and the only one that fires on a lighting cue instead of by hand. Ballrooms, long entrance walks, corporate reveals.

Chauvet CumulusSize 04 · continuous

Runs on distilled water and fluid, refillable while it is running. There is no ice load to run out, so it does not have a stopping point.

The second half of the answer is timing. Dry ice machines need to come up to temperature before they will produce anything, and the ice has to go in close to the moment or it sublimates away doing nothing. So we agree the running order with your planner and your DJ or band in advance, and our technician loads and fires on the cue, not on a guess. The cloud peaks on the beat the song actually starts on. That is a coordination problem, not an equipment problem, and it is the reason this is not a machine you leave switched on in a corner.

When a moment is genuinely too long for one load, or the floor is genuinely too wide for one machine, we do not stretch it. We bring two. Machines can be combined for back-to-back effects, one covering the grand entrance and a second held in reserve for the first dance, or run side by side to cover a larger floor evenly instead of pushing one unit past what it can do.

Low lying fog, running

The layer sits at knee height and stays there. That is the entire trick, and it is a question of temperature rather than of how much fog the machine can make.

Sizing the effect

Four sizes of cloud, and why we own all four

You are not booking four machines. You are booking one, in the size that fits. A rental yard owns a single box and hopes it works for your room. We own the same effect at four different sizes so we can match it to the floor and to the length of the moment, because those two things decide whether the cloud is still there when it matters.

Size 01 · 8 lb load

Nimbus Junior

The compact dry ice machine. Small enough to tuck beside a sweetheart table or at the edge of a chapel aisle where nothing larger will physically fit, and quiet enough that it does not intrude on a ceremony space.

An 8 lb basket is built for one defining moment, a first dance, a ceremony exit, a single reveal, done properly and at full output rather than stretched thin.

Best forIntimate floors, small chapels, tight reception rooms, and any venue where the machine has to disappear into the room.
Size 02 · 12 lb load

Nimbus

The workhorse, and what most of our weddings book. Half again the ice capacity of the Junior, which in practice is the difference between covering a song and covering a sequence.

The longer hold is what lets it carry back-to-back dances, a first dance straight into a father-daughter dance, without the cloud thinning out somewhere in the middle of the second one.

Best forStandard reception dance floors, first dance into parent dances, and most Dallas-Fort Worth wedding venues.
Size 03 · 30 lb load · DMX

ADJ Entour Ice

The largest ice load we carry and the only machine in the fleet on DMX control, which means it fires from the lighting console on a programmed cue rather than from someone reaching for a switch at the back of the room.

That matters when the cue has to land inside a sequence, house lights down, spot up, cloud out, doors open. The timing is written into the show rather than reacted to.

Best forBallrooms, long grand entrance walks, and corporate reveals where the effect is part of a lighting cue stack.
Size 04 · continuous

Chauvet Cumulus

The waterless option, in the sense that there is no ice involved at all. It runs on distilled water and haze fluid, chilling the fog with an onboard system instead of a basket, and it can be topped up while it is running.

Because there is no ice load, there is nothing to run out. It will hold a low layer of atmosphere for as long as you want it there.

Best forAll-night atmosphere, photo and video shoots that need continuous takes, and venues that restrict dry ice on site.

Only one of these comes to your event. The four exist so that the one we bring is the right one. If you already know which size you want, tell us. If you do not, and most people reasonably do not, describe the room and the moment and we will tell you which of the four we would bring and why. That conversation is part of the booking, not an upsell.

Low lying fog machine rental · Dallas-Fort Worth

Low lying fog and dry ice fog machine rental

If you came here searching for a rental rather than an effect, this section is the one written in your language.

There are two very different things being sold in Dallas-Fort Worth under the words “low lying fog machine rental,” and they are almost never distinguished in a listing. It is worth knowing which one you are looking at before you compare anything.

The first is a dry box rental. A party-rental yard hands you a machine for twenty-four hours. The dry ice is not included and is not sourced for you. Setup is not included. Nobody is there to run it. You collect it, you find a supplier who will sell you the right quantity of dry ice on the right day, you transport it, you work out how much to load and when, you load it yourself at the venue, you fire it yourself, and you return the machine. If it does not produce, you find out at the same moment your guests do.

The second is what we do. The machine is delivered, positioned, loaded, cued and operated by our technician, who stays for the event. We source and transport the dry ice. We agree the running order with your planner and your DJ or band beforehand. We place the unit where the output will lay flat across the floor instead of pooling at one edge, and away from detectors and return vents. When the moment comes, someone whose entire job is that cue is standing there watching the floor.

Both are called a rental. Only one of them is a service. We are not the cheapest way to get a fog machine into a room in DFW and we have never tried to be. We are the option for people who want the effect to actually work on the night, on the beat, without it becoming their problem.

Same equipment, several names: low lying fog machine rental, dry ice fog machine rental, ground fog machine, low fog machine, cloud machine rental, dry ice smoke machine. If you searched any of those, you are in the right place, and if you are not sure which one describes what you pictured, describe the picture and we will name it for you.

Wedding fog machine rental

What it looks like at a wedding

This is the reason nearly everyone books it, and there are really only four places in a wedding where it earns its keep.

The effect photographs better than it describes. A knee-deep white layer under a couple, lit from the sides, gives a photographer a clean horizon where there was previously a scuffed dance floor, chair legs and a cable run. It separates the two of you from everything behind you. That is why the first dance photos from a cloud floor look like they were taken somewhere else entirely.

Moment 01

Grand entrance

The cloud runs ahead of you down the walk so you arrive out of it rather than into an empty floor. This is the moment most likely to need the large machine, entrance walks are longer than people expect once introductions are added.

Moment 02

First dance

The classic. The cloud is laid down as the song starts and holds through it. Timing is everything here, which is why our technician takes the cue from your DJ or bandleader rather than guessing at the intro.

Moment 03

Parent dances

Back-to-back with the first dance, and the single most common place a cloud dies early. Covering both from one load is a capacity question, not a luck question. It is exactly what the larger basket is for.

Moment 04

Ceremony exit or last dance

A low layer under a recessional, or under the final song of the night when the floor is full. Quieter uses of the effect, and both of them photograph beautifully.

The cloud also reads colour. If we are already providing uplighting or dance floor lighting, the fog picks the colour up and carries it across the floor, which is a considerably better look than white fog under coloured light that never meets it. When the whole room is designed together, the effect stops looking like an add-on and starts looking like part of the room.

Most couples book this alongside DJ services or as part of a wedding package, which is also the easiest way to get the cue right, when the person calling the fog and the person playing the song work for the same company, the coordination problem stops being a coordination problem.

Beyond weddings

Where else we run the clouds

The same four sizes, matched the same way. What changes is the length of the moment and who is calling the cue.

QuinceañeraThe waltz

A father-daughter waltz across a low cloud is one of the best uses of this effect there is, and the surprise-choreography number that usually follows benefits from it too. Two moments, one after another, which makes this a capacity conversation rather than a machine-choice one.

Birthdays and milestonesThe entrance and the cake

Sweet sixteens, fiftieths, anniversaries. Usually one or two clearly defined moments, the entrance and the cake, which the compact machine handles cleanly without taking over a room that may not be large.

Corporate grand entrances and revealsOn a programmed cue

Product reveals, award walk-ons, keynote entrances. This is where the DMX machine is worth having, because the effect can be programmed into the cue stack with the lighting and the audio instead of being called by hand and landing a second late.

Photo shootsContinuous, take after take

Stills work is unpredictable in length and a dry ice load is not. The continuous machine is almost always the right answer here, refillable while running, so the layer is still there on the fortieth frame as well as the fourth.

Video shoots and music videosHeld for the whole set-up

Same logic, higher stakes, because a video crew resets and reshoots. We will usually recommend the continuous machine for the base layer and hold a dry ice unit for the one hero shot that needs a genuinely dense cloud.

Not sure the effect suits your room?

Some rooms are wrong for it, a heavily air-conditioned space with floor vents will pull the layer apart, and a raised or carpeted floor changes how it behaves. Tell us the venue and we will tell you honestly whether it will look the way you are imagining. If it will not, we will say so and suggest something that will. Questions we get every week

Dry ice and low lying fog, answered

How long does a dancing on the clouds effect last?
For as long as the dry ice load lasts, and no longer. A dry ice machine makes fog by dropping ice into heated water, so output continues while there is ice in the basket and stops when there is not. That is why basket size is the specification that matters, and why we own the effect in four sizes rather than one machine: the 8 lb size is built for one defining moment, the 12 lb size covers back-to-back dances, and the 30 lb size carries a long entrance and still has ice left. The fourth size uses no dry ice at all and has no stopping point. Rather than quote you a number that depends entirely on how hard the machine is run, we ask what moments you want covered and bring the machine that covers them.
What is the difference between dry ice fog and a regular fog machine?
Temperature, and therefore where the fog goes. A standard fog or haze machine produces warm fog, which rises and fills the room, useful for making light beams visible, useless for a cloud effect. Dry ice fog is chilled, so it sinks and stays flat at ankle-to-knee height, holds a defined edge, and dissipates without hazing the room or drifting over the tables. If you want the floor to disappear, you need the cold kind. If you want the air to glow around a lighting rig, you want the warm kind, and those are two different machines.
Do you deliver, set up and run the machine, or is this a pickup rental?
We deliver, set up and run it. This is not a dry-hire and there is nothing for you to collect, load or return. A technician brings the machine, positions it for the room, sources and loads the dry ice, takes the cue from your DJ or bandleader, operates the effect and packs it down afterwards. Most low lying fog listings in Dallas-Fort Worth are twenty-four-hour box rentals with the ice and the setup left to you; that is a genuinely different product, and it is worth checking which one you are comparing us against.
Do I need to buy the dry ice?
No. We source it, transport it and load it, and we bring the right quantity for the machine and for the number of moments you want covered. Dry ice is not something you want to be buying the morning of your wedding: it needs the right supplier, the right quantity, safe handling and correct timing, because it sublimates away whether you are using it or not. Handling all of that is part of the booking.
Is low lying fog safe for guests, the dance floor and the photographer?
It is a widely used effect and we run it with a technician present for exactly this reason. The fog is water vapour chilled by carbon dioxide, it stays low, and it clears on its own. Our technician places the machine so the output lays flat across the floor rather than pooling at one edge, keeps the floor in view for the whole effect, and manages output if the room is behaving differently than expected. Floors can become slightly damp with heavy use, so we place and run it with that in mind, and we will always talk through anything specific to your venue or your guests beforehand.
Will the fog set off the venue's smoke detectors?
We will not tell you it cannot happen, because any airborne effect can interact with a detector. What we do is clear the effect with the venue in advance and, where the venue uses one, with their alarm monitoring company, and then place the machines away from detectors and return air vents. Many venues have a defined process for fog effects and simply need notice; some restrict dry ice entirely, which is one of the reasons we own a machine that does not use it. Tell us the venue early and we will handle that conversation before the date rather than on it.
Can we use the cloud effect for the grand entrance and the first dance?
Yes, and this is exactly the situation that decides which machine we bring. Two separated moments need either one large load or two machines. We can combine machines for back-to-back effects, with one covering the grand entrance and a second held in reserve for the first dance, or run two side by side to cover a larger floor evenly rather than pushing a single unit past what it can do. Tell us every moment you want the cloud on and we will build the plan around all of them instead of hoping one load stretches.
Do you rent low lying fog machines outside of weddings?
Regularly. Quinceanera waltzes, milestone birthdays, corporate grand entrances and product reveals, photo shoots and video shoots. The corporate reveals usually run on our DMX machine so the effect fires inside a programmed lighting cue, and shoots usually run on the continuous machine because a camera crew resets more often than a dry ice load allows. Same fleet, same technician, same approach. We ask what the moment is and bring the machine that fits it.
